Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, let’s keep it really simple. Think of your choices in three main buckets:

Type of rose plant

Where and how it will grow

Extra helpers (other plants & products)

Type of rose plant

These are the big “shapes” or jobs roses can have:

Climbing roses:

Grow tall and long
Need a fence, trellis, arch, or wall
Great if you want a “rose-covered” entry or backdrop

Shrub/bush roses:

Rounded shape, like a medium to big bush
Good for most gardens and along borders
Nice choice for beginners; very versatile

Hybrid tea roses (classic long-stem style):

The classic “florist-style” rose on long stems
Great if you want flowers for cutting and putting in vases

Groundcover/landscape roses:

Low and spreading
Good for covering space, edges, or slopes
Often lower maintenance and bloom a lot
Where and how it will grow

There are two big things to think about here:

Sunlight:

Full sun = 6+ hours of direct sun per day. Most roses want this.
Partial shade = about 4+ hours of sun. Some roses and perennials can handle this.

Hardiness zone:

This is how cold your winters get.
On our site you can choose your zone at the top; it will show plants that can live in your climate.

So: first ask, “Where will this go?” Fence, pot, bed by the front door, etc. That quickly narrows the type.

Extra helpers (other plants & products)

Perennials:

Non-rose plants that come back every year, like lavender, catmint, daisies, etc.
These look beautiful mixed with roses and help fill in around them.

Bulbs:

Things you plant mainly in fall for spring blooms (like tulips and daffodils).
These give you color before your roses really get going.

Soil amendments & fertilizers:

Soil amendments (like compost or manure) improve your soil so roots are happier.
Fertilizers feed the plant so you get more growth and blooms.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. Let’s keep it simple.

For a beginner, you really just need:

The basics
A sunny spot outdoors (ideally 6+ hours of direct sun)
Decent, well‑drained soil
A shovel or trowel
Access to water (hose or watering can)
Mulch (helps keep roots cool and moisture in)
Optional but very helpful: soil amendments These improve the soil around your new rose. They are not required, but they make getting started easier for the plant.
Bone meal: Helps strong root development.
Cow manure: Adds long‑lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Improves soil structure and aeration; can be mixed into the planting area or used as a top layer to protect roots.
Worm castings: Gentle, nutrient‑rich material that improves soil and feeds the plant slowly.

You can plant without these, but using one or two often helps new gardeners get better results.

Fertilizer (this one is important) Fertilizing is needed for long‑term health and good blooming.
We offer fertilizers like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer, and also Boost & Bloom.
You are not limited to our brands; any rose‑appropriate fertilizer works.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is usually easiest for beginners to use and adjust.

Planting roses: Planting Roses
General how‑to library: How‑to Articles & Videos
